title: Introduction
content:
Introduction Context and Motivation In today’s API-driven ecosystem, organizations require application interfaces that are highly available, secure, and capable of handling unpredictable workloads without the overhead of managing physical infrastructure. Ensuring optimal performance while protecting against abuse, malicious attacks, and unauthorized access is a critical challenge for modern API deployments.
The project “Serverless API Gateway with Advanced Security and Rate Limiting” presents a scalable and secure serverless API solution, leveraging the power of Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and a suite of AWS security services. This architecture is designed to deliver reliable performance under high traffic while implementing robust, multi-layered security controls and intelligent request throttling to maintain system stability.
Incoming client requests are routed through Amazon API Gateway, where usage plans, API keys, and rate limiting policies are applied to control traffic. Authentication and authorization are managed via Amazon Cognito or JWT tokens, while AWS WAF provides advanced protection against DDoS, bots, and malicious payloads. All API business logic is executed in stateless AWS Lambda functions, and persistent data is stored in Amazon DynamoDB or Aurora Serverless. Logging, metrics, and request tracing are handled by Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray.
Key Benefits of Serverless API Gateway with Advanced Security and Rate Limiting By integrating AWS services such as API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, CloudWatch:
Scalable and cost-efficient API management: Automatically scales to handle thousands of concurrent requests with pay-as-you-go pricing. Multi-layered security: Combines authentication, authorization, encryption, and threat filtering. Traffic control and abuse prevention: Usage plans and throttling protect resources from overload. Robust monitoring and diagnostics: Real-time insights with CloudWatch metrics, logs. Simplified operations: No server management, easy deployment, and quick updates to API logic. Global accessibility with low latency: Deployable in multiple AWS Regions to serve users worldwide efficiently.

title: Serverless API Gateway And Advanced Security And Rate Limiting
content:
Serverless API Gateway with Advanced Security and Rate Limiting 📌 Overview In modern applications, APIs act as the communication bridge between services and applications. To meet demands for performance, security, and scalability, the serverless architecture on AWS API Gateway combined with AWS Lambda offers an optimal solution.
In addition to handling high traffic volumes, the system should apply advanced security mechanisms and rate limiting to protect resources, prevent abuse, and ensure a stable user experience.
🧩 Architecture Description This solution is built on AWS serverless services, operating without the need to manage physical servers, with the following workflow:
API Gateway
Serves as the single entry point for all client requests. Implements rate limiting via API Gateway Usage Plans and API Keys to control maximum requests per second and set daily/monthly quotas. Advanced Security
Authentication & Authorization: Uses Amazon Cognito or JWT tokens to authenticate users. Protection against DDoS and Bots: Integrates AWS WAF to filter malicious traffic and block harmful IPs. Data Encryption: Uses HTTPS/TLS for data in transit and AWS KMS for encrypting sensitive data at rest. Lambda Functions
Executes business logic for the API. Stateless deployment that automatically scales based on traffic load. Database
Amazon DynamoDB or Aurora Serverless for high-performance and scalable data storage. Monitoring & Logging
Amazon CloudWatch Logs and Metrics for logging and API performance monitoring. AWS X-Ray for analyzing and tracing request flows. 🌐 Deployment Scope The entire architecture is deployed in AWS Region Singapore (ap-southeast-1) to optimize latency and comply with local data residency requirements.
🔒 Solution Advantages Auto Scaling: The API can serve thousands of concurrent requests without manual infrastructure adjustments. Multi-layered Security: Combines Cognito, WAF, KMS, and HTTPS/TLS. Intelligent Traffic Control: Prevents abuse and protects resources through rate limiting and quotas. Flexible Cost Model: Pay per API request and Lambda execution time. Advanced Monitoring & Analytics: Monitor API performance and behavior in real time. title: Environment Setup
content:
Guide to Setting Up a Serverless Development Environment on AWS To deploy, manage, and develop Serverless solutions on AWS, you need to prepare the following tools. This guide applies to Windows, macOS, and Linux.
1. Install AWS CLI (Command Line Interface) AWS CLI allows you to manage AWS services via the command line.
Windows Download the AWS CLI installer for Windows Double-click the downloaded AWSCLIV2.msi file and follow the instructions to install. After installation, open Command Prompt and check: aws --version macOS Download the AWS CLI installer for macOS Double-click the downloaded AWSCLIV2.pkg file and follow the instructions to install. After installation, open Terminal and check: aws --version Linux (x86_64) Open Terminal and run the following commands: curl "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" -o "awscliv2.zip" unzip awscliv2.zip sudo ./aws/install Check the installation: aws --version If the command returns the version, AWS CLI is installed successfully.
2. Install Node.js (Version 20 or higher) Node.js provides the JavaScript runtime needed for AWS CDK and deployment scripts.
Download Node.js:
Visit https://nodejs.org/en/download/ Choose the LTS or Current version (must be >= 20.x.x) Follow the installation instructions for your OS. Check installation:
node --version Ensure the version is >= 20.x.x
3. Install AWS CDK (Cloud Development Kit) AWS CDK lets you define AWS infrastructure as code.
Install via npm:
npm install -g aws-cdk Check installation:
cdk --version If the version is returned, CDK is installed successfully.
4. Configure AWS CLI to Connect to Your AWS Account After installing AWS CLI, configure your AWS credentials.
Run the configuration command: aws configure Enter the following information when prompted: AWS Access Key ID: Enter your Access Key (from IAM in AWS Console) AWS Secret Access Key: Enter your Secret Key Default region name: For example, ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) or your preferred region Default output format: json (or yaml, text) Note:
Do not share your Access Key/Secret Key. If you don’t have them, create new ones in IAM > Users > Security credentials.
5. Verify AWS CDK Connection to Your AWS Account After configuration, check the connection with:
List existing stacks: cdk ls If the command returns a stack list or does not show authentication errors, you have configured successfully.
6. (Recommended) Install Additional Tools Git: Source code management (Download here) Visual Studio Code: Powerful code editor (Download here) AWS Toolkit for VS Code: Extension for managing AWS directly from VS Code. Summary After completing these steps, you are ready to develop, deploy, and manage Serverless solutions

title: Create New Project
content:
Guide to Creating a New AWS Serverless CDK Project (TypeScript) This section provides a detailed step-by-step guide to create a demo CDK project (TypeScript), install the necessary packages, and prepare the environment for synth/deploy. You can copy and paste the command blocks into your terminal as needed.
1. Create the project folder and move into it mkdir aws-serverless-demo && cd aws-serverless-demo Purpose: Create a dedicated folder to keep CDK files, Lambda code, configuration, and other resources organized.
2. Initialize the CDK project with TypeScript cdk init app --language typescript This command scaffolds a CDK project using TypeScript, creating default folders and files like bin/, lib/, package.json, tsconfig.json, etc.
3. Install required dependencies Run the following command in your project directory:
npm install aws-cdk-lib @aws-cdk/aws-apigatewayv2 @aws-cdk/aws-apigatewayv2-integrations @aws-cdk/aws-lambda-nodejs @aws-cdk/aws-dynamodb @aws-cdk/aws-iam jsonwebtoken @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb constructs esbuild Brief description of the packages:
aws-cdk-lib: CDK v2 library (L1/L2 constructs) @aws-cdk/aws-apigatewayv2 & @aws-cdk/aws-apigatewayv2-integrations: Constructs for HTTP/WebSocket API @aws-cdk/aws-lambda-nodejs: Supports building Lambda Node.js with esbuild @aws-cdk/aws-dynamodb: Constructs for DynamoDB @aws-cdk/aws-iam: Constructs for creating IAM Roles/Policies jsonwebtoken: Handle JWT in Lambda @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb: AWS SDK v3 for DynamoDB constructs: Runtime dependency for CDK esbuild: Fast build tool for Lambda Node.js Note: Some modules like API Gateway V2 may be in alpha state depending on the CDK version.
4. (Optional) Install devDependencies for TypeScript If cdk init did not already add them:
npm install --save-dev typescript ts-node @types/node 5. Bootstrap CDK Only needed once per account/region.
Default: cdk bootstrap Specify account/region: cdk bootstrap aws://<ACCOUNT_ID>/<REGION> --profile <PROFILE_NAME> Example:
cdk bootstrap aws://123456789012/ap-southeast-1 --profile MyProfile Bootstrap will create the S3 bucket, roles, and SSM parameters needed for CDK deploy.
6. Add utility scripts to package.json "scripts": { "build": "tsc -p tsconfig.json", "watch": "tsc -w -p tsconfig.json", "synth": "cdk synth", "deploy": "cdk deploy", "destroy": "cdk destroy" } npm run build: Compile TypeScript npm run synth: Generate CloudFormation template npm run deploy: Deploy stack to AWS npm run destroy: Delete stack and resources 7. Initial checks Compile TypeScript:
npm run build Generate template:
npm run synth Deploy (if already bootstrapped and AWS CLI configured):
npm run deploy -- --profile <PROFILE_NAME> 8. Recommended folder structure aws-serverless-demo/ ├─ bin/ │ └─ aws-serverless-demo.ts ├─ lib/ │ └─ aws-serverless-demo-stack.ts ├─ package.json ├─ tsconfig.json └─ cdk.json 9. Common issues Node.js version: >= 20 CDK CLI & aws-cdk-lib: Should be version-matched Credentials error: Check aws configure or AWS_PROFILE Lambda bundling error: Ensure esbuild is installed Conclusion After completing these steps, you are ready to develop and deploy AWS Serverless applications with CDK

title: Create Serverless
content:
Write Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with AWS CDK In this step, we will write Infrastructure as Code to deploy the entire serverless infrastructure, including:
DynamoDB (on-demand) Lambda Authorizer (custom JWT) Lambda Handler (API logic) HTTP API Gateway with authorizer, caching, usage plan, and API key 1. Create or edit the file lib/aws-serverless-demo-stack.ts import * as cdk from 'aws-cdk-lib'; import { Construct } from 'constructs'; import * as apigw from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-apigatewayv2'; import * as integrations from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-apigatewayv2-integrations'; import * as lambda from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs'; import * as dynamodb from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-dynamodb'; import * as iam from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-iam'; export class AwsServerlessDemoStack extends cdk.Stack { constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: cdk.StackProps) { super(scope, id, props); // DynamoDB Table (on-demand for demo) const table = new dynamodb.Table(this, 'DemoItemsTable', { partitionKey: { name: 'id', type: dynamodb.AttributeType.STRING }, billingMode: dynamodb.BillingMode.PAY_PER_REQUEST, }); // Lambda Authorizer (custom JWT, not using Cognito) const authorizerLambda = new lambda.NodejsFunction(this, 'DemoAuthorizerLambda', { entry: 'lambda/authorizer.ts', handler: 'handler', runtime: lambda.Runtime.NODEJS_20_X, environment: { JWT_SECRET: 'demo-secret-key-12345', // Replace with a real secret for production }, }); // Lambda Handler (Handles GET/POST logic with validation) const handlerLambda = new lambda.NodejsFunction(this, 'DemoHandlerLambda', { entry: 'lambda/handler.ts', handler: 'handler', runtime: lambda.Runtime.NODEJS_20_X, environment: { TABLE_NAME: table.tableName, }, }); table.grantReadWrite(handlerLambda); // HTTP API Gateway (cheaper than REST API) const httpApi = new apigw.HttpApi(this, 'DemoHttpApi', { apiName: 'ServerlessDemoApi', }); // Authorizer const authorizer = new apigw.HttpLambdaAuthorizer('DemoJwtAuthorizer', authorizerLambda, { authorizerName: 'DemoJwtAuthorizer', identitySource: ['$request.header.Authorization'], }); // Integration const lambdaIntegration = new integrations.HttpLambdaIntegration('DemoLambdaIntegration', handlerLambda); // Routes (/items GET/POST with auth) httpApi.addRoutes({ path: '/items', methods: [apigw.HttpMethod.GET, apigw.HttpMethod.POST], integration: lambdaIntegration, authorizer: authorizer, }); // Caching for GET (TTL 60s) const stage = httpApi.defaultStage as apigw.HttpStage; const cachePolicy = new apigw.CachePolicy(this, 'DemoCachePolicy', { defaultTtl: cdk.Duration.seconds(60), enableAcceptHeader: true, }); stage.node.addDependency(cachePolicy); // Usage Plan + API Key (rate limit: 1000 req/min, quota 10000/day) const usagePlan = httpApi.addUsagePlan('DemoUsagePlan', { name: 'DemoPlan', throttle: { rateLimit: 1000, burstLimit: 2000 }, quota: { limit: 10000, period: apigw.Period.DAY }, }); const apiKey = httpApi.addApiKey('DemoApiKey'); usagePlan.addApiKey(apiKey); usagePlan.addApiStage({ stage: httpApi.defaultStage! }); // Outputs for demo new cdk.CfnOutput(this, 'ApiUrl', { value: httpApi.url! }); new cdk.CfnOutput(this, 'ApiKeyId', { value: apiKey.keyId }); } } 2. Edit the file bin/aws-serverless-demo.ts #!/usr/bin/env node import 'source-map-support/register'; import * as cdk from 'aws-cdk-lib'; import { AwsServerlessDemoStack } from '../lib/aws-serverless-demo-stack'; const app = new cdk.App(); new AwsServerlessDemoStack(app, 'AwsServerlessDemoStack', {}); ✅ After finishing, you can run:
cdk synth cdk deploy The system will deploy the entire serverless infrastructure on AWS.

title: Write Code for Lambda Functions
content:
Write Code for Lambda Functions In this step, we will write the source code for the AWS Lambda Functions that serve the API Gateway.
1. Create the lambda folder In the root directory of your project, create a folder to store the Lambda code:
mkdir lambda 2. File lambda/authorizer.ts — JWT Authentication This Lambda acts as an Authorizer for API Gateway, using JSON Web Token (JWT) for authentication.
import * as jwt from 'jsonwebtoken'; export const handler = async (event: any) => { const token = event.headers?.Authorization?.split(' ')[1]; if (!token) return denyPolicy(); try { jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET!); return allowPolicy(event.methodArn); } catch (err) { return denyPolicy(); } }; function allowPolicy(methodArn: string) { return { principalId: 'user', policyDocument: { Version: '2012-10-17', Statement: [{ Action: 'execute-api:Invoke', Effect: 'Allow', Resource: methodArn }], }, }; } function denyPolicy() { return { principalId: 'user', policyDocument: { Version: '2012-10-17', Statement: [{ Action: 'execute-api:Invoke', Effect: 'Deny', Resource: '*' }], }, }; } 3. File lambda/handler.ts — Business Logic & Validation This Lambda handles the logic for GET and POST requests to the API.
import { DynamoDBClient, PutItemCommand, ScanCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb'; const client = new DynamoDBClient({}); export const handler = async (event: any) => { const method = event.httpMethod; const tableName = process.env.TABLE_NAME!; if (method === 'POST') { try { const body = JSON.parse(event.body); if (!body.id || !body.name) { // Request validation return { statusCode: 400, body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Missing id or name in body' }) }; } await client.send(new PutItemCommand({ TableName: tableName, Item: { id: { S: body.id }, name: { S: body.name } }, })); return { statusCode: 201, body: JSON.stringify({ message: 'Item created successfully' }) }; } catch (err) { return { statusCode: 500, body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'POST failed' }) }; } } else if (method === 'GET') { const result = await client.send(new ScanCommand({ TableName: tableName })); return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify(result.Items || []) }; } return { statusCode: 405, body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Method Not Allowed' }) }; }; ✅ After completing these two files, your Lambda functions will:
Authenticate requests using JWT. Support two methods: POST: Add an item to DynamoDB. GET: Retrieve a list of items from DynamoDB. Return appropriate HTTP status codes and clear error messages.

title: Deploy Stack to AWS
content:
Deploy Stack to AWS A detailed step-by-step guide to synth and deploy your CDK stack to AWS, retrieve outputs (ApiUrl, ApiKeyId), and get the actual API Key value for testing the API.
1. Preflight Checks Before deploying, make sure you have installed and configured all required tools, and are in your project directory (where cdk.json is located):
# Check AWS CLI / credentials aws --version aws sts get-caller-identity --profile <PROFILE_NAME> # Check Node & npm node --version npm --version # Check CDK CLI & project build cdk --version npm run build # if using TypeScript; or `npm run build` as defined in package.json aws sts get-caller-identity will show the Account and ARN of the credentials in use — use this to verify you are deploying to the correct account.
2. Bootstrap the CDK environment If the account/region has not been bootstrapped (first time using CDK for that account/region), run one of the following:
# Default bootstrap (uses default profile) cdk bootstrap # Bootstrap for a specific account/region and profile cdk bootstrap aws://<ACCOUNT_ID>/<REGION> --profile <PROFILE_NAME> Example:
cdk bootstrap aws://123456789012/ap-southeast-1 --profile NhatTruong Note: cdk bootstrap only needs to be run once per account/region. It creates the S3 bucket, IAM roles, and SSM params required for deployment.
3. Synthesize the template — cdk synth Build TypeScript (if needed) and synth:
npm run build # build TS to JS (if your project uses TS) cdk synth --profile <PROFILE_NAME> cdk synth will print out the CloudFormation template. If you encounter compile or import errors, fix your code before deploying.
4. Deploy the stack — cdk deploy A. Standard deploy:
cdk deploy --profile <PROFILE_NAME> B. Deploy and save outputs to a JSON file :
cdk deploy --outputs-file cdk-outputs.json --profile <PROFILE_NAME> During deployment, CDK may prompt for confirmation (Are you sure? Type “y”). Type y to continue. Deployment time: about 2–5 minutes (depending on resources and region). C. Example:
cdk deploy --outputs-file outputs.json --profile NhatTruong After deployment, the outputs.json file will contain the Outputs defined in your stack (e.g., ApiUrl, ApiKeyId).
5. Retrieve outputs from terminal or output file A. From the terminal:
At the end of the CDK deploy, you will see an Outputs section like:
Outputs: AwsServerlessDemoStack.ApiUrl = https://abc123.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com AwsServerlessDemoStack.ApiKeyId = a1b2c3d4e5f6 B. From file (if you used –outputs-file):
Open cdk-outputs.json (or outputs.json) and find the values for ApiUrl and ApiKeyId.
6. Get the actual API Key value The API Key ID (ApiKeyId) is not the value the client needs — the client needs the API key value (the secret string).
A. Via AWS Console (UI) Open AWS Console → API Gateway. In the left menu, select API Keys. Find the API Key by ApiKeyId (the ID matches the CDK Output). Open the key, click Show to reveal the API key value. Copy this value and use it as the x-api-key header when calling the API. B. Via AWS CLI There are two ways (use the correct region and profile):
Method 1 - Get a key by ID:
aws apigateway get-api-key --api-key <API_KEY_ID> --include-value --profile <PROFILE_NAME> --region <REGION> The JSON result will contain a value field with the actual API key.
Method 2 - List all keys with values (filter with jq):
aws apigateway get-api-keys --include-values --profile <PROFILE_NAME> --region <REGION> | jq '.items[] | {id:.id, name:.name, value:.value}' Use jq to filter id, name, value and select the key you need. Example with profile NhatTruong and region ap-southeast-1:
aws apigateway get-api-key --api-key a1b2c3d4e5f6 --include-value --profile NhatTruong --region ap-southeast-1 7. Test the API A. GET /items (use API key and JWT in Authorization header) curl -i -X GET "https://<API_HOST>/items" -H "x-api-key: <API_KEY_VALUE>" -H "Authorization: Bearer <JWT_TOKEN>" B. POST /items curl -i -X POST "https://<API_HOST>/items" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "x-api-key: <API_KEY_VALUE>" -H "Authorization: Bearer <JWT_TOKEN>" -d '{"id":"1","name":"Demo Item"}' Note: If your authorizer uses a custom JWT, you need a valid token (signed with the JWT_SECRET configured in the Lambda authorizer or generated by your system).
8. Monitor logs & quick troubleshooting View Lambda logs:
Go to CloudWatch → Logs → Log groups → find the group for your Lambda (named after your Stack). Or use AWS CLI to view log events. Common errors and quick fixes:
Credential/account mismatch: Run aws sts get-caller-identity --profile <PROFILE_NAME> to check the account. Use the correct --profile when bootstrapping/deploying. CloudWatch Logs role ARN must be set: If API Gateway reports a missing CloudWatch role ARN, go to API Gateway → Settings → CloudWatch log role ARN and create/assign the APIGatewayPushToCloudWatchLogs role (or use CLI to attach the role + policy). Lambda bundling errors: Make sure esbuild is installed; check error output for missing modules. “Constructor is not a constructor”: Check export/import in bin/ and lib/ (named export vs default export). 9. Cleanup resources When you no longer need the stack, delete it to avoid incurring costs:
cdk destroy --profile <PROFILE_NAME> Or delete individual resources from the Console if you want to keep some components.
10. Timing & final notes Deployment time: ~2–5 minutes for a small demo; may take longer if the bundle is large or the network is slow. Always check CDK outputs and save ApiUrl + ApiKey somewhere safe for testing. For automation, use cdk deploy --outputs-file with CI (GitHub Actions, CodePipeline, etc.). Done: After these steps, your API will be live, you will have an API key for testing, and you can monitor everything via CloudWatch.

title: Monitoring Configuration and API Documentation
content:
Configure and Check Monitoring (CloudWatch Logs) AWS automatically enables monitoring for both Lambda Functions and API Gateway, making it easy for you to track and debug.
1. Check Logs Open the AWS Management Console. Navigate to CloudWatch. Select Log groups. Find the log groups: /aws/lambda/DemoHandlerLambda /aws/apigateway/DemoHttpApi/... (the full name will include the API Gateway ID) Click on the log group to view detailed logs. 2. Set Log Retention Period By default, AWS retains logs indefinitely, which can increase storage costs. You should limit the log retention period.
In the log group you want to configure: Select Actions > Edit retention. Choose 7 days (or another value that fits your needs). Click Save. 💡 Tip: Only keep logs for as long as necessary to save costs.
Create Documentation with OpenAPI/Swagger You can export your API Gateway configuration in OpenAPI 3 format to generate clear API documentation.
1. Export OpenAPI Spec from AWS Console Go to AWS Console > API Gateway. Select the ServerlessDemoApi API. Choose Stages > default. Click Export. Select Export as OpenAPI 3. Choose Export as YAML and save the file. 2. Import into Swagger UI Open Swagger Editor at: https://editor.swagger.io/ Select File > Import file. Upload the exported YAML file or copy its contents into the editor. View and check endpoints, authentication, and descriptions. 💡 You can edit the YAML in Swagger Editor to add descriptions, examples, or more detailed information.
✅ Result: You will have a visual API document that is easy to share with developers or testers to understand and use

title: Testing with Postman, Curl, and Unit Test
content:
1. Generate JWT Token for Testing In this demo environment, our Lambda Authorizer uses JWT with the secret a-string-secret-at-least-256-bits-long and algorithm HS256.
You need to generate a valid token to test your requests.
Steps to generate a token: Go to https://jwt.io/. In the Header section, enter: { "alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT" } In the Payload section, enter: { "sub": "1234567890", "name": "John Doe", "admin": true, "iat": 1516239022 } In the Secret section: Secret: demo-secret-key-12345 Copy the generated token to use in Postman. 💡 You can set the token expiry as you wish (e.g., 15 minutes for demo). 2. Unit Test (Jest) Install Jest npm install --save-dev jest ts-jest @types/jest Configure Jest for TypeScript (if not already) npx ts-jest config:init Create file lambda/handler.test.ts import { handler } from './handler'; test('GET should return 200', async () => { const response = await handler({ httpMethod: 'GET' }); expect(response.statusCode).toBe(200); }); test('POST with invalid body should return 400', async () => { const response = await handler({ httpMethod: 'POST', body: '{}' }); expect(response.statusCode).toBe(400); }); Run unit tests npx jest 3. Integration Test with Postman 3.1. GET (Check caching, auth, API Key) Add Token: Add the generated JWT token. Add key: Add the API key obtained from AWS Console > API Gateway > API Keys > Select key by ID > Show “API key”. 3.2. POST (Check validation) Add Token: Add the token as above. Add key: Add the API key as above. Add Data: Add sample data to test the POST method. { "id":"demo1", "name":"test-item" } 3.3. Test Rate Limit using PowerShell or Terminal Use a script to send >1000 requests/minute: 1..1100 | ForEach-Object { $headers = @{ "Authorization" = "Bearer eyJhbGciOiJ....." "x-api-key" = "VOj............" } try { $response = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://rlkzdtjind.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/prod/items" -Method Get -Headers $headers -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue if ($response.StatusCode -eq 200) { Write-Output $response.StatusCode } } catch { Write-Output $_.Exception.Response.StatusCode.Value__ } } | Out-File -FilePath "output.txt" Run the script: Run in PowerShell or Terminal. Expected result: 1100 requests without hitting the rate limit. Open the output.txt file to check the results, there should be no 429 errors (Rate Limit Exceeded). 3.4. Test Invalid JWT Send a request with an invalid JWT or leave the Authorization header empty: Expect 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden. ✅ Expected results:
Unit tests pass. GET/POST work correctly with auth + API Key. Cache works → latency decreases on the second call. Rate limit

title: Resource Cleanup
content:
Cleanup to Avoid Unwanted Charges After completing your tests and demo, you should delete all resources created on AWS to avoid incurring unexpected costs.
1. Delete the CDK Stack Run the following command in your project directory:
cdk destroy Confirm yes when prompted. This command will delete all resources created by AWS CDK (Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, IAM Role, etc.). 2. Delete CloudWatch Logs (optional for extra savings) Go to the AWS Console. Navigate to CloudWatch → Log groups. Find and select related log groups, for example: /aws/lambda/DemoHandlerLambda /aws/lambda/DemoAuthorizerLambda /aws/apigateway/ServerlessDemoApi/... Choose Actions → Delete log group → Confirm. ⚠ Note:
If you forget to run cdk destroy, resources like DynamoDB, API Gateway, or CloudWatch Logs will continue to exist and incur
